summary: Martin Harrysson and Natasha Maniar from McKinsey's Software X practice address the disconnect between AI's individual productivity gains and enterprise-level outcomes. While developers report tasks shrinking from days to minutes, surveyed enterprises average only 5-15% productivity improvements. 70% of surveyed companies haven't changed roles at all, creating a gap between expectations and actual role definitions. The speakers identify bottlenecks: unchanged collaboration patterns, manual code reviews overwhelmed by AI-generated code, tech debt amplification, inefficient work allocation, and fuzzy story specifications producing unintended code. Most companies remain stuck in Agile-era operating models—8-10 person teams, two-week sprints—designed for human development constraints. McKinsey surveyed 300 enterprises and found top performers are 7x more likely to deploy AI-native workflows (scaling 4+ use cases across the SDLC) and 6x more likely to adopt AI-native roles (smaller pods, consolidated roles). These organizations achieved 5-6x increases in time-to-market and delivery speed. AI-native workflows mean continuous planning replacing quarterly planning and spec-driven development replacing story-driven work. AI-native roles mean one-pizza pods of 3-5 product builders orchestrating agents with full-stack fluency. One client reorganized from two-pizza teams to smaller pods with consolidated roles, creating more pods from the same headcount while maintaining or improving code quality and accelerating output. Different engineering functions require different operating models: legacy modernization suits a factory-of-agents model, while greenfield work benefits from iterative co-creation loops. Scaling across hundreds of teams requires getting 20-30+ change management interventions right simultaneously—communication, incentives, upskilling, and measurement. A tech company example showed AI tool usage dropping off without proper change management, requiring a reset with hands-on upskilling, coaches, and measurement systems. Another client used code labs and certifications to drive adoption. Bottom performers don't measure speed and only 10% measure productivity. McKinsey proposes a holistic measurement framework spanning inputs (tool investment, upskilling resources), outputs (adoption velocity, developer NPS, code quality, security, resiliency via mean time to resolve priority bugs), and economic outcomes (time to revenue, price differentiation, customer expansion, cost reduction per pod). The speakers conclude by urging organizations to start now, set bold ambitions, and find the right model for their context.

sections.title: Introduction and the AI Productivity Gap
sections.summary: Martin and Natasha introduce McKinsey's Software X practice and frame the talk around people and operating model changes needed for AI in software development. They compare the current AI paradigm shift to the transition to Agile 20 years ago. Despite individual productivity gains, a survey of 300 enterprises shows only 5-15% average productivity improvements, revealing a disconnect between potential and reality.

sections.title: Bottlenecks Limiting AI Value
sections.summary: The speakers identify emerging bottlenecks: unchanged collaboration patterns, manual code reviews overwhelmed by AI-generated code, tech debt amplification, inefficient work allocation due to variable task and person effectiveness with AI, and fuzzy story specifications producing unintended code. These bottlenecks keep large companies stuck in marginal gains within Agile-era operating models.

sections.title: AI-Native Workflows and Roles
sections.summary: Survey findings show top performers are 7x more likely to have AI-native workflows (4+ use cases across SDLC) and 6x more likely to have AI-native roles, yielding 5-6x delivery speed improvements. AI-native workflows mean continuous planning and spec-driven development. AI-native roles mean one-pizza pods of 3-5 product builders replacing separate specialized engineers. Different engineering functions need different operating models: factory-of-agents for legacy modernization, iterative co-creation for greenfield work.

sections.title: Banking Case Study and Role Transformation
sections.summary: A leading international bank tested team-level interventions: agent-assisted sprint assignment, co-created prototypes with security/observability criteria, workflow-based squad reorganization, and PMs directly observing customer feedback. Results included 60x increase in agent consumption and 51% increase in code mergers. The speakers note engineers must shift from code execution to agent orchestration and work decomposition.

sections.title: Scaling, Change Management, and Measurement
sections.summary: 70% of surveyed companies haven't changed roles at all. One client reorganized from two-pizza teams to smaller pods with consolidated roles, creating more pods from the same headcount while maintaining or improving code quality and speed. Scaling across hundreds of teams requires getting 20-30+ change management interventions right simultaneously. A tech company example showed AI tool usage dropping off without proper change management, requiring a reset with hands-on upskilling, coaches, and measurement. Another client used code labs and certifications. Bottom performers don't measure speed and only 10% measure productivity. McKinsey proposes a holistic measurement framework spanning inputs (tool investment, upskilling), outputs (adoption, developer NPS, code quality, security, resiliency), and economic outcomes (time to revenue, price differentiation, cost reduction per pod). The speakers conclude by urging organizations to start now, set bold ambitions, and find the right model.
